newsitem.title: USA: U.S. soy crush at six-month low on slumping demand.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soy crush at six-month low on slumping demand.

text.p: Falling feed and export demand and scheduled spring maintenance at crushing facilities helped push the pace of the weekly U.S. soybean crush to the lowest level since October, soymeal brokers said.
"I think demand is dropping off more than people think," said one southeastern broker. "We're seeing more and more feed substitution and exports are going to be down sharply."

According to data supplied by the National Oilseed Processors Association, the crushing pace of 25.938 million bushels reported for the week ended April 9 was the lowest since the October 10-reported pace of 25.623 million.
The weekly crush was lower than expected and surprised many in the trade, whose estimates ranged from 26.32 million to 27.2 million bushels. The previous week's NOPA crush was 27.87 million bushels.
"I had no idea we would be this low," said another southeast broker. "I can't find that many shut-downs to justify (a drop of) two million bushels."
Many soybean processors are starting to take scheduled down-time for maintenance this month, but closures have generally only lasted several days to a week, dealers said.
However, most in the trade had expected the large slowdown to come next week, when many more processors were believed to be scheduling down-time.
The soymeal market's high prices have forced some livestock producers to turn to less expensive sources of feed for their animals, which has also limited demand, dealers said.
Soymeal prices recently soared near eight-year highs.
Meal for May delivery on the Chicago Board of Trade closed Friday at $274.80 per ton.
Trade in peanut meal, cottonseed meal and meat and bone meal all became more active in late winter, brokers said.

"Cottonseed meal is $100.000 per ton cheaper (than soymeal) right now," one broker said. "With only six or seven percent less protein, they don't have to feed that much more to make up the difference."
Cottonseed meal has a protein content of 41 percent compared with soymeal's protein content of 47.5 to 48 percent.
Because cottonseed contains less protein, hog and poultry producers have to use more in feed rations, the broker said.
Some in the trade also pointed to falling export demand as a reason for the soybean crushing slowdown.
Net export sales this week were a respectable 85,700 tonnes, but much of the outstanding business is optional origin and could be switched to South America, dealers said.
"We're almost absolutely through about 90 percent of the exports that are on the books," said a Tennessee-based broker. "What's left is also optional origin."
The weekly crushing pace has trended lower since March 12, but the U.S. Department of Agriculture did not reflect the slowdown in Friday's Supply and Demand Report.
USDA left its 1997 crushing forecast of 1.420 billion bushels unchanged.
"To me, yesterday's crush was still consistent for a crop year crush of 1.420 billion bushels," said Dale Gustafson, analyst with Smith Barney in Chicago.
Gustafson said he expected the weekly soy crush pace next month to fall to a weekly average of 23.5 million bushels.
